# Specific and latent heat (`latent_specific_heat`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs thermometer_temperature
- Core idea: Different substances need different amounts of heat for the same rise in temperature; water has a high specific heat (about ten times as much as iron, weight for weight). Melting and boiling swallow large amounts of heat with no rise in temperature at all: melting ice takes as much heat as warming the same water from 0 to 80 degrees, and turning boiling water into steam takes more than five times what was needed to bring it from freezing to the boil. That is why ice lasts, why steam scalds worse than boiling water, and why an engine that cools and reheats its cylinder at every stroke wastes most of its fuel.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming ice at 0 degrees turns to water as soon as it reaches 0
  - Treating heat and temperature as the same thing
  - Expecting water to get hotter the harder it is boiled
- History: europe: c. 1757–1762 Joseph Black (Glasgow) establishes latent and specific heat in lectures; 1764–1765 Watt applies it to the steam engine; 1772 Wilcke publishes independently; 1780s Lavoisier and Laplace's ice calorimeter
- Read:
  - Joseph Black, Lectures on the Elements of Chemistry (1803)
  - D. S. L. Cardwell, From Watt to Clausius (1971)
